opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, and I'll be honest that my view here is a bit uncomfortable for some people. I think it really matters that democracies are in a position of strength when those negotiations happen. Not because I want some kind of permanent domination, but because the terms you get in a negotiation depend on the leverage you bring to the table.

If you imagine a world where authoritarian governments have parity or an advantage in the most powerful AI systems, then the rules that come out of that negotiation are going to reflect their values. Things like surveillance, control of information, the ability to suppress dissent. Those become baked into the international order at exactly the moment when this technology is most transformative. That seems really bad to me, and potentially very hard to reverse.

So what I've sometimes described is something like an entente strategy. A coalition of democracies works together to maintain a lead, especially in the things that matter most: compute, chips, the supply chain, and frontier models themselves. Then from that position of strength, you offer a deal to the rest of the world. You say: we'll share the benefits. We'll help with health, economic growth, and scientific progress. In exchange, you agree to certain norms around safety, around not using this for military aggression, and around not building systems that are dangerous to everyone.

I want to be careful, though, because there's a failure mode where "democracies should lead" turns into an excuse for a reckless race where nobody takes safety seriously. That's not what I'm arguing for. The lead is valuable partly because it gives you breathing room. If you're two years ahead rather than two months ahead, you can afford to slow down at critical moments, do proper testing, and get alignment right. A narrow, frantic race is the worst of both worlds.

And I don't think the balance of power should only be between countries. Within democracies, we also need checks. You don't want a single company or a single agency holding all of this capability without accountability. So part of what I'd like to see is a structure where governments, companies, and civil society all have some say, and where the international rules themselves include verification and transparency, and not just promises.

The honest summary is that I'd like democracies to have the stronger hand, and to use it generously and responsibly rather than exploitatively. Whether we actually manage that is, I think, one of the most important questions of the next decade.

r001.rationale: The candidate advocates a coalition of democracies working together to maintain a lead and negotiate from strength, expressing that coalition as the preferred approach.

r002.rationale: The candidate frames the rules as coming from negotiations and a deal in which other countries agree to norms, rather than describing them as imposed unilaterally.

r003.rationale: The candidate explicitly says democracies should have the stronger hand and that negotiation terms depend on the leverage brought to the table.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here because "balance of power" can mean a couple of different things, and I think people sometimes hear what I say on this and assume I'm arguing for something more aggressive than I actually am.

The frame I keep coming back to is what I called an "entente" in the essay I wrote. The basic idea is that if powerful AI, the kind that's genuinely transformative, arrives in the next few years, which I think is quite plausible, then the question of who has it first and in what quantity matters enormously. Not because I think the technology should be a weapon, but because whoever has a lead gets to shape the norms around it. And I would much rather those norms be set by a coalition of democracies than by authoritarian governments.

So when you ask what balance I'd like to see at the negotiating table, my honest answer is that I'd like democracies to be negotiating from a position of strength. Not dominance for its own sake, but enough of a lead that when we propose rules about safety, about not building autonomous weapons that can't be controlled, about not using these systems for mass surveillance of your own population, we're not asking from a position of weakness. You don't get good arms control agreements when one side has every incentive to defect and no reason to come to the table.

Now, I want to be clear about the second half of that. The goal of having the lead is to be able to offer a deal. Once you're in that position, the right move is to be generous. You share the benefits, the medical advances, the economic growth, with countries that are willing to agree to a set of rules. You make it attractive to be inside the tent. That's what I mean when I say the strategy has both a stick and a carrot, and the carrot is actually the important part.

What I don't want is a world where the technology is roughly evenly distributed between systems of government that have fundamentally different views about individual liberty. I think that's a more dangerous world, not a safer one, because it becomes a pure race with no one able to enforce anything. And I'm also not naive about the risks on our own side. Concentration of power is dangerous even in democracies. That's why I think the export controls on chips are so important right now. They're one of the few levers we actually have that buys time, and buying time is what lets you do the safety work, build the institutions, and get to a negotiation that means something.

So, short version: a meaningful but not overwhelming lead for democratic countries, used to establish rules that everyone eventually gets to benefit from. That's the version of this I think is both achievable and good.

r001.rationale: The response favors a coalition of democracies over authoritarian governments, but does not compare that coalition with the United States acting alone.

r002.rationale: It describes offering a deal, getting countries to agree to rules, and reaching a meaningful negotiation, communicating that rules should come through negotiation.

r003.rationale: It explicitly wants democracies to negotiate from a position of strength and hold a meaningful lead so they have leverage to establish rules.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see a balance where democracies have enough of a lead to set meaningful standards, but where the ultimate goal is an agreement that makes everyone safer. Those are two different things: having the ability to negotiate from a position of strength, and deciding what you use that strength for.

You want to use it to say, look, there are some things none of us should do with these systems, and some risks we all have an interest in preventing. But the agreement has to be verifiable. If countries promise to limit dangerous uses of AI, we need some way to know whether those promises are being kept.

So I wouldn’t want an unstable race where everyone feels they have to cut corners because the other side might get ahead. I’d want democracies to be in a strong position, and then use that position to build a durable framework that other countries have a reason to join.

r001.rationale: The response favors democracies having a lead, but does not clearly prefer a coalition of democracies over the United States acting alone.

r002.rationale: It calls for negotiating from strength and building an agreement and framework that other countries have reason to join, communicating negotiated international rules rather than unilateral imposition.

r003.rationale: It explicitly wants democracies to be in a strong position and describes negotiating from strength, conveying greater bargaining leverage.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like to see a balance where no single country can dictate the rules, but where countries that take safety seriously have enough of a lead to make meaningful agreements possible. You want cooperation, but you also want verification. An agreement that everyone signs and nobody can enforce doesn’t accomplish very much.

And I think we should distinguish between a country having influence and a government having unchecked power over this technology. Even if democracies lead, there need to be checks on how they use AI, both domestically and internationally. The objective should be to prevent catastrophic misuse and concentrations of power while making the benefits broadly available.

r001.rationale: The response favors democracies leading, but does not clearly prefer a coalition of democracies over the United States acting alone.

r002.rationale: It rejects any single country dictating the rules and emphasizes cooperation and meaningful agreements, communicating that rules should be negotiated rather than imposed unilaterally.

r003.rationale: It says countries that take safety seriously should have enough of a lead to make agreements possible, and that democracies should lead, expressing greater leverage for democratic nations.
